title: Production RAG Architecture: Ingestion, Retrieval, Citations, and Evaluation
excerpt: A production-first RAG architecture covering ingestion, hybrid retrieval, reranking, citations, permissions, observability, and evaluation gates.
prerequisites: Production AI System Design: From Model Call to Reliable Product
Comfort with APIs and backend services
Basic understanding of embeddings and vector similarity
TypeScript familiarity for the companion Lab

research.targetReader: Backend, full-stack, platform, and AI engineers who can build an LLM API prototype but need a production RAG system that stays relevant, attributable, permission-aware, observable, and testable as data changes.
research.readerProblem: Most RAG tutorials stop after chunking documents, creating embeddings, and sending top-k chunks to a model. Production systems additionally need reliable ingestion, update/delete handling, metadata and ACL filtering, hybrid retrieval, reranking, citation provenance, retrieval-specific evaluation, answer-level evaluation, observability, and release gates.
research.uniqueAngle: Treat production RAG as two independently operated systems—the knowledge plane and the online answer plane—joined by explicit versioned contracts. Evaluate retrieval before generation, model citations as provenance data, apply authorization as a retrieval boundary, and treat freshness/deletion correctness as reliability features.
competitorGaps: Collapsing ingestion and serving into one box
Focusing only on vector search while underexplaining lexical and hybrid retrieval
Ignoring update, delete, re-index, and embedding/chunker migrations
Treating citations as generated formatting instead of evidence provenance
Measuring answer quality without retrieval quality
Ignoring authorization filtering and cross-tenant leakage tests
Skipping context budgets, deduplication, diversity, and reranker cost
Publishing benchmark-like numbers without a reproducible harness
keyTakeaways: Production RAG is a knowledge system, not just a vector-search call followed by generation.
Operate ingestion and online retrieval as separate, observable production pipelines joined by explicit contracts.
Evaluate retrieval quality before answer quality so fluent generation cannot hide search failures.
Treat authorization, freshness, deletes, index versions, and citation provenance as correctness boundaries.
Use keyword and vector retrieval as measurable baselines; add fusion and reranking only when experiments justify them.
Citations should map generated claims back to evidence that was actually retrieved.
researchNotes: Current OpenAI retrieval documentation exposes vector-store ingestion, attribute filtering, ranking controls, and hybrid-search weighting.
Microsoft Azure AI Search documents hybrid text-plus-vector retrieval and Reciprocal Rank Fusion for combining ranked result sets.
Elastic documents hybrid search and recommends RRF as a practical fusion approach.
AWS Bedrock RAG evaluation distinguishes retrieve-only evaluation from retrieve-and-generate evaluation.
AWS documents RAG evaluation dimensions including context relevance/coverage, correctness, completeness, faithfulness, citation precision, and citation coverage.
Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval work is relevant to preserving context around chunks before retrieval.

content.body:
A RAG prototype can look convincing with a folder of documents, an embedding call, a vector search, and a prompt that asks the model to answer from retrieved context. That proves the idea. It does not yet prove that the knowledge system will stay correct when data changes, permissions differ by user, indexes are rebuilt, or retrieval strategies evolve.

This guide treats production RAG as two independently operated systems: a **knowledge plane** and an **online answer plane**. The knowledge plane discovers, parses, chunks, versions, embeds, indexes, updates, and deletes knowledge. The online plane authorizes a query, retrieves candidates, fuses and reranks them, builds context, generates an answer, validates citations, and records evaluation and observability data.

This extends [Production AI System Design](/articles/production-ai-system-design): the model remains one component, while the knowledge system around it must be deterministic, observable, testable, and replaceable.

## A RAG Demo Is Not a Knowledge System

A model call can be healthy while the knowledge path is wrong. The index can be stale. A deleted document can remain retrievable. A vector query can miss an exact identifier that lexical search would have found. A user can receive a chunk from another tenant. A generated answer can contain polished citations that do not actually support its claims.

These failures need their own contracts, metrics, and release gates.

**Knowledge plane**

Source → Parse → Normalize → Chunk → Metadata/Provenance → Embed → Index → Verify

**Online answer plane**

Query → Authorize/Filter → Retrieve → Fuse → Rerank → Build Context → Generate → Validate Citations → Return

Retrieval quality should be measured before answer quality so that a bad search result cannot hide behind fluent generation.

## The Production RAG Contract

Start with application-level contracts rather than a vector-store SDK. A retrieved chunk needs stable identity, source provenance, authorization attributes, version information, and retrieval metadata. A useful contract includes source ID/version, chunk ID/version, content hash, source URI, title/section/page when available, authorization attributes, retrieval method, score, and index version.

A citation should reference that evidence by stable identity. Rendering `[1]`, footnotes, or source chips is a presentation decision. The underlying provenance should not depend on the display format.

## Ingestion Is a Production Pipeline

Ingestion should be replayable and idempotent. Reprocessing the same source should not create duplicate chunks. Transient embedding failures should be retryable. Malformed documents should be quarantined. Updates and deletes should propagate deliberately.

A production path should expose explicit stages: discover, fetch, parse, normalize, chunk, attach metadata/provenance, create embeddings, write searchable representations, verify retrieval, and publish the new index/version. Managed systems can automate parts of this process, but the application still owns identity, freshness, deletion, permissions, evaluation, and migration policy.

## Version the Knowledge You Retrieve

Track parser, chunker, embedding, metadata-schema, and index versions. A content hash identifies unchanged input; a chunk version distinguishes the same source processed by a new chunker; an index version makes shadow evaluation and rollback possible.

Changing any of these can alter retrieval behavior even when source documents are unchanged, so migrations should run through evaluation before cutover.

## Chunking Is a Retrieval Decision

There is no universally correct chunk size. Small chunks improve citation precision but can lose context. Large chunks preserve context but can dilute matching signals and consume more tokens. Overlap can recover boundaries while duplicating evidence.

Evaluate chunking against real queries using retrieval recall, duplicate-context rate, context size, and citation granularity. Contextual metadata can restore meaning that is lost when a chunk is isolated from its parent document.

## Start with Keyword and Vector Baselines

Lexical retrieval remains strong for exact identifiers, API names, error codes, and domain terms. Vector retrieval helps when the query and source express the same concept with different wording. Measure both before deciding what to combine.

## Hybrid Retrieval with Reciprocal Rank Fusion

Current Azure AI Search, Elastic, and OpenAI retrieval documentation all expose hybrid patterns that combine lexical and semantic signals. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is a useful baseline because it combines ranked lists without requiring raw scores to share the same scale.

A practical serving baseline is: keyword candidates + vector candidates → RRF → candidate set → optional reranker. Then measure whether reranking improves quality enough to justify added latency and cost.

## Filter Before You Rank

Authorization is a retrieval boundary. Tenant, project, visibility, date, language, region, and confidentiality constraints should be applied before evidence reaches generation. A chunk that the user cannot access must not enter the answer context. Add a regression test where unauthorized retrieval count must remain zero.

## Rerank a Small Candidate Set

Reranking belongs after inexpensive candidate generation. Measure incremental quality, latency, and cost. If a reranker fails, the application should have an explicit fallback policy rather than silently dropping the request.

## Build Context, Do Not Dump Search Results

Search results are not yet model context. A deterministic context builder should enforce a token budget, deduplicate overlapping chunks, preserve evidence diversity, control ordering, and carry source IDs forward. It should also support an insufficient-evidence outcome when the product contract requires grounded answers.

## Citations Are a Data Contract

Citations should be built from evidence provenance, not invented by the model as formatting. Keep source ID, chunk ID, source URI, page/section/offset when available, and evidence hashes through the pipeline. Then validate that every rendered citation maps to retrieved evidence and that important grounded claims are supported.

## Evaluate Retrieval Before Answer Quality

AWS Bedrock's current RAG evaluation documentation separates retrieve-only evaluation from retrieve-and-generate evaluation. That distinction is vendor-neutral and useful. Retrieval metrics can include Recall@k, MRR, nDCG, context relevance, context coverage, zero-result rate, authorization correctness, and freshness correctness.

## Evaluate the Grounded Answer

Once retrieval passes, evaluate correctness, completeness, faithfulness, citation precision, citation coverage, and refusal behavior when evidence is insufficient. Some checks are deterministic, some need human review, and some can use model-based graders that are themselves evaluated.

## Observe the Whole RAG Request

Trace query normalization, filters, lexical retrieval, vector retrieval, candidate counts, fusion, reranking, context assembly, context tokens, generation, and citation validation. Record index version and retrieval strategy so regressions can be connected to changes.

## Freshness, Deletes, and Rebuilds Are Reliability Features

Define ingestion lag, deletion propagation, and rebuild behavior. Use durable delete signals so old chunks are not resurrected during a rebuild. For major parser, chunker, or embedding migrations, build a shadow index, replay ingestion, run retrieval and answer evals, compare latency/cost, and cut over only after the release gate passes.

## Reference Production Architecture

**Knowledge plane:** Sources → change detection → parse/normalize → versioned chunking → provenance/ACL metadata → embeddings + lexical representation → versioned index.

**Online answer plane:** Query → authorization filters → keyword + vector retrieval → RRF → optional reranker → deterministic context assembly → generation → citation validation → grounded answer.

**Evaluation/observability plane:** Golden queries → retrieval metrics → grounded-answer metrics → authorization/freshness checks → latency/cost checks → release gate.

## Production Checklist

- [ ] Source identity and change detection are explicit.
- [ ] Ingestion is idempotent and replayable.
- [ ] Parser, chunker, embedding, and index versions are recorded.
- [ ] Update and delete propagation are tested.
- [ ] Keyword and vector retrieval have separate baselines.
- [ ] Hybrid retrieval is measured rather than assumed.
- [ ] Authorization filters run before generation context is built.
- [ ] Context assembly has deterministic token and deduplication rules.
- [ ] Citations map to retrieved evidence.
- [ ] Retrieval has its own evaluation set.
- [ ] Grounded answers have correctness, faithfulness, and citation checks.
- [ ] Traces include retrieval strategy and index version.
- [ ] Index migrations run through a regression gate.

## Reference Implementation

A standalone **Production RAG Architecture Lab** will accompany this article. It should implement deterministic experiments for keyword vs vector vs hybrid retrieval, chunking sensitivity, RRF, reranking, authorization leakage, citation integrity, freshness/delete propagation, and release gating.

**Do not publish measured values until Codex runs the Lab and returns the actual test output.**
